vignette:
The abuse began when she was seven. Her father, a man respected in their close-knit community, would beat her with a leather belt in the small back room of their apartment. She learned to stand perfectly still, arms at her sides, while he struck her back and legs. She never cried afterward—she learned that too. What stayed with her, what she could never put into words even now at fifty-one, was the way her body would lock into that same rigid posture whenever a memory surfaced, as if she were back in that room, waiting for the next blow. The rage that followed was silent and white-hot, a fury she had no name for as a child and no outlet for as an adult.

Nadia worked for a social ministry in a low-income neighborhood, coordinating food assistance and housing referrals. The job required her to meet one-on-one with clients in a small office with a desk and two chairs. She had been doing it for six years, but after her divorce three years ago, something shifted. She began to notice that when a male client closed the door behind him, her chest would tighten. She would feel her arms go still at her sides, her spine straighten. The memory was not a story she could tell—it was a position her body assumed, a rage that rose without warning. She started leaving the office door slightly ajar during meetings. When that felt insufficient, she began scheduling all appointments in the communal waiting area, even though it meant less privacy for the clients. She told herself it was for transparency, but she knew, deep down, that she was watching the door.

Her vigilance grew. She found herself checking behind her when walking to her car, scanning parking lots for figures that might be following her. She would react to a sudden knock on her office door with a full-body startle, her heart hammering, even when she knew it was just a coworker. These false alarms exhausted her. She became irritable with colleagues, snapping at them for small things—a misplaced file, an unexpected question. She knew her reactions were outsized, but in the moment, the danger felt absolute. She had come to believe that she could never be truly safe, that the world was full of men who might, at any moment, take her into a small room and hurt her.

The more vigilant she became, the more her body remembered. Each time she checked behind her, each time she positioned herself near an exit, she felt the ghost of that childhood posture—arms straight, back rigid, waiting. The checking fed the memory, and the memory demanded more checking. She stopped agreeing to home visits with male caseworkers. She began leaving work early to avoid the empty hallway at dusk. She never allowed herself to be alone with a man in any enclosed space, not even the elevator in her apartment building. She would wait for the next car, or take the stairs. Her social world shrank. Her ex-husband had moved on, and she had few friends left; she was too quick to anger, too easily spooked, too preoccupied with exits.

What finally brought her to the clinic was a moment in her own kitchen. She had been chopping vegetables when a neighbor knocked on her door—a man she knew, asking to borrow a tool. She froze, knife in hand, and for a split second she was seven years old again, belt in the air, body locked. She could not open the door. She stood there until he went away, and then she sat on the floor and wept. She was afraid of what she was becoming. She was afraid that her own life had become a small, locked room.
